documentation.range: This species is endemic to the state of Sonora, Mexico and is found in  the northern portion of the state near El Dátil, Altar District, near Sierrita de López and Sierra Jojoba (Gentry 1982).
documentation.population: Agave fortiflora is a rare plant that has a limited distribution with few individuals, known with certainty only from the presumed type locality in the Sierra Jojoba and near the Sierrita de López (Gentry 1982). None of the subpopulations have been relocated (Gentry 1982, Klopper et al. 2010).
documentation.habitats: Agave fortiflora is found in plains and on ridges in northern Sonora in vegetation of desert scrub on limestone substrate. The last time it was observed by Gentry (1982), he noted that the rosettes produced offsets sparingly, and old or extensive colonies are rare.
documentation.threats: This species grows in an area impacted by cattle ranching, so it could potentially be threaten by this activity.
documentation.measures: This species does not occur in protected areas. The specimens found in ex-situ collections in 7 botanical garden worldwide (BGCI 2019) are very likely mis-identifications given the scarcity of the species (W. Hodgson pers. comm. 2019). There are live specimens grown from seed at the Desert Botanical Garden, Phoenix from the subpopulation observed by agave enthusiasts Etter and Martin in 2001. Specimens collected by Felger, Sue Carnahan have been determined as a putative hybrid between Agave angustifolia var. angustifolia and A. colorata, and not A. fortiflora, with which it may be confused (Felger et al. 2017, S. Felger pers. comm. 2019).
documentation.use_trade: This agave is used by Tohono O'ohdam Indians pit-baked as food (Gentry 1982). It is doubtful that this species is being sold in nurseries but specimens referred as A. fortiflora are found in trade; it is very likely, if not definitely, that these are being misidentified, especially if the original source is coastal Sonora. It is believed that the species has not been found nor documented since Gentry (W. Hodgson pers. comm. 2019).
documentation.rationale: Since the species was first found by Gentry (1972) the population has been seen only once in 2001 by Etter and Martin and the identification of this observation is still unconfirmed. Several expeditions have been conducted in the area and the species has not been reported. The species has an area of occupancy of 8 km<sup>2</sup> and one location where the population was reported to have few individuals and the threat from cattle ranching is suspected given that the overall area where the species grow is affected by this activity. The species is here listed as Critically Endangered Possibly Extinct in the Wild and would benefit from further research.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Agave fortiflora Gentry is distinguished by its light grey glaucous leaves with a finely tuberculate rugose texture and large, long-lasting flowers with a short perianth tube that is broad and bulging at the place of attachment of the filaments (Gentry 1982). The species does not show relation to other members of Gentry’s Ditepalae, although he assigned it to the group. There was some doubt to the origin of the type specimen with its initial description (Gentry 1972) due to loss of the garden tag at Huntington Botanical Garden. Comparisons of the leaf anatomy (cuticle, epidermis and stomata) of his original leaf collection at Sierra Jojoba with that of the Huntington plant confirmed to Gentry that the two specimens are specifically alike (Gentry 1982). 

Collections with flowering material from near Bahía San Carlos (Gentry & Engard 23560) definitely place that subpopulation with Agave colorata, not with A. fortiflora as was previously reported by Gentry (1972, Gentry 1982). Gentry (1982) also adds that plants with atypical linear-lanceolate leaves from a canyon site, north of Bahía San Carlos belong to a subpopulation of A. colorata.  Agaves determined as a hybrid between A. angustifolia var. angustifolia and A. colorata (Felger et al. 2017) occur in the vicinities of Cañón del Nacapule and San Carlos, and the north end of Sierra El Aguaje. Gentry’s banded and narrow, long-leaved form of Agave colorata in a palm canyon north of San Carlos Bay might involve this putative hybrid (R. Felger pers. comm. 2019).

documentation.habitats: This species occurs in semi- or full shade in East African highlands.
documentation.threats: There has been extensive habitat loss due to agricultural activities (crop cultivation). There are proposed development plans for much of the area.
documentation.measures: Makonde Scarp Forest Reserve occurs close by, but it is not clear if this species occurs within the reserve or not. It is also not known from ex situ collections (BGCI 2018).
documentation.use_trade: There is no information about use or trade of this species.
documentation.rationale: This species is known only from the type collection made in 1959. There have been subsequent collecting trips in the area but to date it has not been re-found. The area has been extensively impacted by agricultural activities, and there are proposed development plans in the area. It seems reasonable to infer that, if the species still exists, it has a very small population and is presumably very restricted. The area of occupancy (AOO) is 4 km2 and its extent of occurrence (EOO) could not be calculated as it is only known from one locality. It is here assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct).

documentation.range: Lophura edwardsi is endemic to central Viet Nam. Known historically from four provinces (Ha Tinh, Quang Binh, Quang Tri and Thua Thien Hue), it was formerly described as locally fairly common. Individuals were recorded near to the Phong My Commune, Thua Thien Hue, and also near the Huong Hiep Commune, Quang Tri (Le Trong Trai et al. 1999). Several other individuals were found in the Quang Tri and Thua Thien Hue Provinces, but the last confirmed recent record was in 2000, where one male was confiscated from a hunter and held in captivity in the Hai Lang District Forest Protection Department, Quang Tri. It has been suggested that the species may have historically occurred in Lao PDR, but this remains unconfirmed and if it was once present, it is now almost certainly extinct given hunting pressure, which is even more acute in Lao PDR than Viet Nam (Timmins et al. 2024).
documentation.population:
The last confirmed records of L. edwardsi were in 2000, when a juvenile male was captured in February, and two males, a female and four eggs were reported in March (Eames and Mahood 2017). A purported female was photographed in 2009 but was identified as a female Silver Pheasant Lophura nycthemera (R. Dams in litt. 2023, J. Eaton in litt. 2023). A male with a deformed beak, also supposedly photographed in 2009, is not considered to be a genuine record (R. Dams in litt. 2023).

Lophura 'hatinhensis', which was previously described as a species, is a mutation of L. edwardsi that has been observed at either end of, and within, the known range of, L. edwardsi  (J. Eames in litt. 2012, Hennache et al. 2012). The occurrence of birds showing inbred characteristics since the 1960s and the lack of any recent records of the species are an indication that any remaining populations would be extremely small, fragmented and declining. Similarly, the description of another invalid taxon, Imperial Pheasant Lophura imperialis, a L. nycthemera x L. edwardsi hybrid, suggest the population size has been small for some time.

Following methods developed in a series of papers published in 2017 (Akcakaya et al. 2017, Keith et al. 2017, Thompson et al. 2017), the probability that this species is extinct based on records and surveys is 0.973, and the probability it is extinct based on threats is 0.873. The minimum population size is therefore set to 0 mature individuals, while the upper limit is arbitrarily set to <50 mature individuals, recognising that if this species is extant, any remnant population must be tiny.
documentation.habitats: L. edwardsi is confined to 'exceedingly damp' evergreen lowland forest below 300 m, characterised by year-round high humidity, high rainfall and a thick understory rich in lianas (N. Brickle in litt. 2004).
documentation.threats:
Threats for this species have operated at an acuity and spatial scale that may have driven it extinct. Using the threats extinction probability model devised by Keith et al. (2017), the probability the species is extinct based on threats is 0.873 (BirdLife International, unpubl. data).

The two main threats faced by L. edwardsi are habitat loss and degradation, and hunting, primarily with snares. L. edwardsi is thought to be confined to 'everwet' evergreen lowland forest below 300 m in the Central Annam region of Viet Nam (Eames and Mahood 2017). However, this lowland habitat has been extensively deforested and replaced almost entirely with irrigated rice cultivation (Eames and Mahood 2017). Remaining forest suffered acute and extensive defoliation during the American-Vietnam War, during which 72 million litres of herbicide were sprayed on Vietnamese forests (Eames et al. 1992) and continues to be exploited through commercial logging, firewood collection, charcoal production and fragrant oil extraction (Robson et al. 1991, Eames et al. 1992, BirdLife International 2001). Selective logging and the near-total removal of the largest trees has had an extensive impact on the structure and associated microclimates of forest remnants, and the thinning of the canopy and degradation of the understory is thought to have led to the drying of the ‘everwet’ forest on which L. edwardsi relies (Timmins et al. 2024). 

The use of wire snares for hunting is a pervasive and insidious threat across South-East Asia (Gray et al. 2018, 2021). Hunters erect multiple drift fences that extend for hundreds, if not thousands, of metres with snares placed along them every few metres (Holden 2005). Terrestrial birds and mammals are killed indiscriminately. Such techniques are employed not only by professional hunters but also by rattan collectors, loggers, gold miners and fragrant oil extractors, exerting an immense hunting pressure on wildlife (Eames et al. 1992, Le Manh Hung et al. 2004). Snaring occurs across Viet Nam on an almost industrial scale. For example, between 2011 and 2019 around 127,000 wire snares were removed from the 320 km2 Hue-Quang Nam Saola Reserves alone (Gray et al. 2021). Regardless of such intense persecution, other Galliformes such as Gallus gallus and L. nycthemera seem to be somewhat more tolerant of this hunting pressure than L. edwardsi (Brickle et al. 2008). The tolerance of other species to hunting suggest that hunting pressure is not solely responsible for decline but instead is the coup de grâce following an extensive loss of suitable habitat and microclimate.

The description of what transpired to be two invalid taxa in the 20th century is somewhat indicative of L. edwardsi having a small population size for quite some time, likely a result of the historical clearance of lowland forest. L. imperialis is a naturally occurring hybrid between L. edwardsi and L. nycthemera, while L. hatinhensis is an inbred form of L. edwardsi (Hennache et al. 2012). Hybridisation with L. nycthemera, may threaten the genetic integrity of remaining L. edwardsi and competition with this congener (which is more plastic in habitat use) may also pose a threat (BirdLife International 2001).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions Underway
Listed in CITES Appendix I. An Action Plan was published for this species in 2015 (Pham Tuan Anh and Le Trong Trai 2015).

Surveys for the species were conducted on foot in 1988, 1990, 1991, 1994, 2002 and 2004 (Eames et al. 1988; Robson et al. 1991; Eames et al. 1992; Eames et al. 1994; Le Manh Hung et al. 2002; Le Manh Hung et al. 2004). From 2005 to 2023, extensive camera trap surveys were carried out across Viet Nam by a number of organisations including VietNature, WWF and Re:wild (R. Dams and Le Trong Trai in litt. 2023, Nguyen Quang Hoa Anh in litt. 2023, A. Tilker in litt. 2023). In that time, it is estimated that there have been at least 500,000 camera trap nights of surveys within the potential range of L. edwardsi. The localities from which the most recent records derive have been incorporated into the Phong Dien, Dakrong and Ke Go protected areas, for which management feasibility studies have been completed (Le Trong Trai 1999). Bac Huong Hoa. Khe Net and Khe Nuoc Truong have also been proposed as protected areas (Pham Tuan Anh and Le Trong Trai 2015). Site Support Groups have been established for Dakrong IBA and Bac Huong Hoa IBA.

In December 2003, the captive population numbered 1,033 individuals (A. Hennache in litt. 2004) and in December 2023 it was estimated to be close to 1,400 birds (R. Dams in litt. 2023). A project investigating the feasibility of reintroductions is underway with aviaries under construction to facilitate the programme. The maternal line has been screened and hybrids purged from the captive stock (A. Hennache in litt. 2004). Poster distribution and community interviews have occurred since 2014 around Trurong Son, but there has been little information gained from these about the persistence of the species in this location.

Conservation Actions Proposed
Use remote sensing to classify forest according to humidity in order to identify potentially suitable areas for the species within the remaining forest matrix (Eames and Mahood 2017). Conduct further surveys of remaining forest fragments within and to the north of its historical range using camera trapping and specially trained dogs (Eames and Mahood 2017), particularly at areas identified through modelling approaches (e.g. Grainger et al. 2017), to clarify the species status and ecological requirements. Establish the proposed Phong Dien and Dakrong Nature Reserves, encourage the protection of other key sites for the species (Pham Tuan Anh and Le Trong Trai 2015) and enhance Site Support Groups. Promote careful management of captive Vietnamese Lophura pheasants through the ISB system, and regularly review ex-situ measures until their taxonomic relationships are clarified. If appropriate, utilise the captive population to prepare suitable individuals for reintroduction (Pham Tuan Anh and Le Trong Trai 2015, R. Dams in litt. 2023). Prepare a landscape level management plan to redress genetic problems caused by habitat fragmentation and establish effective habitat protection. Assess the level and impact of hunting and campaign for its control, starting with complete cessation in protected areas holding the species. Conduct research to establish the feasibility and effects of using forest corridors to connect forest fragments.
documentation.use_trade: Trapped for food using wire snares and drift fences; although not targeted specifically, snares are indiscriminate (Gray et al. 2018, 2021; Timmins et al. 2024). Captive individuals are occasionally kept by local people and birds were exported to Europe as display animals in the early to mid-20th century, the descendants of which form much of the ex-situ conservation breeding population as well as those kept by private aviculturists. Birds have not been taken from the wild for ex-situ breeding for a number of decades.
documentation.rationale: Following methods developed in a series of papers published in 2017 (Akcakaya et al. 2017, Keith et al. 2017, Thompson et al. 2017), the probability that the species is extinct based on records and surveys is 0.973, and the probability it is extinct based on threats is 0.873. Although this generates an average extinction probability of 0.92, the threats models does not meet the threshold for Extinct. Accordingly, it is classified as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct). There have been no recent records of Lophura edwardsi despite extensive surveys, suggesting that any remaining wild population is likely to be extremely small and severely fragmented. Population declines have been driven by high levels of hunting pressure and lowland forest clearance and degradation.
documentation.trend_justification: The species is suspected to have declined rapidly from a combination of hunting and habitat loss, given that virtually all forest habitat within its range has now been lost and remaining fragments are under intense pressure. L. edwardsi has likely always been rare. There were 22 individuals recorded from its discovery in 1895 to 1935, most of which were taken as specimens (Eames and Mahood 2017). The species was next seen in 1964, with 24 records of 62 individuals seen between then and 2000 (Eames and Mahood 2017). Only one bird was recorded in the 1960s, one in the 1970s, three in the 1980s, 53 in the 1990s and four birds were seen in 2000 (BirdLife International 2001, Eames and Mahood 2017). The two males (one of which was captured), a female and four eggs are considered the last genuine records of the species (Eames and Mahood 2017). The absence of records since, despite considerable survey effort (R. Dams in litt. 2023), indicates that the population has continued to decline, and the probability it is extinct is estimated at greater than 90% (following methods in Akcakaya et al. [2017], Keith et al. [2017], and Thompson et al. [2017]).
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Lophura edwardsi (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously split as L. edwardsi and L. hatinhensis following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993). Lophura imperialis (Sibley and Monroe 1990, 1993) is considered a hybrid between Silver Pheasant Lophura nycthemera and Vietnam Pheasant L. edwardsi following Rasmussen (1998), Garson (2001) and BirdLife International (2001).

documentation.range: This species is endemic to the Hawaiian islands, historically known from around 1,200 meters elevation on the island of Moloka'i.
documentation.population: The last known individual was seen in 2014, but was dead in 2015.
documentation.habitats: The taxon is a short-lived, scandent, climbing, perennial herb found in Hawaiian montane wet forest dominated by ʻōhiʻa (Metrosideros polymorpha).
documentation.threats: The major threats to this taxon include direct competition by invasive non-native plant species, especially Melinis minutiflora, Buddleia asiatica, Rubus rosifolius, and Schinus terebinthifolia, and predation by non-native animals, particularly pigs and slugs. Feral pigs also degrade habitat. In addition, the taxon is threatened by landslides, disease (powdery mildew), and insect pests (root mealybugs). Fortini et al, (2013) characterized this taxon as moderately vulnerable to climate change (vulnerability index 0.564).
documentation.measures: The taxon is on the US Endangered Species List, and also on the State of Hawai'i Endangered Species List. Ex situ micropropagation is the only living representation remaining for this taxon. Outplantings have not yet been attempted. Further exploration of suitable habitat is needed to confirm its extinct in the wild status.
documentation.use_trade: There are no known uses for this species.
documentation.rationale: Stenogyne bifida is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild). The taxon is endemic to the island of Moloka'i and has an extent of occurrence of zero km2. It has experienced severe decline in habitat and numbers due to the impacts of invasive plants and animals. Its area of occupancy is zero km2. Its habitat includes extremely remote rugged terrain that makes it difficult to confirm extinction. This qualifies the taxon to a ranking of Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) under criteria C and D.

documentation.range: This species is endemic to the Hawaiian islands, at 790 m elevation in the Waiʻanae mountains on the island of Oʻahu.
documentation.population: The taxon is extremely rare (possibly extinct in the wild), with a total known population of zero individuals.
documentation.habitats: The taxon is a perennial subshrub that was found in Hawaiian lowland mesic forests.
documentation.threats: The major threats to this taxon include direct competition by invasive non-native plant species, especially Erigeron karvinskianum, Melinis minutiflora, Morella faya, Passiflora suberosa, and Schinus terebinthifolia; as well as predation and habitat degradation by non-native animals, particularly pigs and goats. Fortini et al. (2013) did not characterize the climate change vulnerability of this taxon.
documentation.measures: The taxon is on the US Endangered Species List, and also on the State of Hawaiʻi Endangered Species List. The last known subpopulations occurred in protected areas, but were not fenced. Ex situ cultivation and seed storage is also ongoing. Outplantings have occurred in a fenced exclosure, but have not yet yielded viable offspring. Further research is needed on general ecology, life history, and population genetics.
documentation.use_trade: There are no known uses for this species.
documentation.rationale: Silene perlmanii is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild). The taxon was endemic to the island of Oʻahu and, being last observed in 1997, has an extent of occurrence of zero km2. It had experienced severe and ongoing decline in habitat and numbers due to the impacts of invasive plants and animals. It is in cultivation and seed storage. This qualifies the taxon for a ranking of Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) under criterion D.

documentation.range: This species is endemic to Indonesia. Based on GBIF (2020) there is only one location in East Kalimantan, Berouw, Mt. Ilas Bungaan (1957). The species has an area of occupancy of 4 km<sup>2</sup>.
documentation.population: There is no population information available for this species.
documentation.habitats: This is a tree of unknown height recorded only from limestone areas.
documentation.threats: The species is likely to be threatened for a number of reasons including karst mining and also conversion of all surrounding habitat to agriculture. Other human activities such as development of industry may also have had an impact on the species.
documentation.measures: A survey is needed to confirm if the species is still known from its one locality, as it was last collected in 1957. The species may be found in collections at the Botanical Garden of Mulawarman University.
documentation.use_trade: There is no information on use and trade of the species.
documentation.rationale: This species is endemic to Kalimantan, Indonesia. It is known from a single collection. The one known locality of the species is located in an area completely converted to agriculture and the preference of the species to karst environments puts it at risk of limestone quarrying. It is therefore likely that the species is no longer present in the wild. It was first collected in 1957 and has not been collected since. The small area of occupancy and decline in habitat supports assessment of the species as Critically Endangered, Possibly Extinct in the Wild.

documentation.population: <span id="docs-internal-guid-9c4f46ee-7fff-cd8f-dce8-2439f37cfd05">The taxon is extremely rare and possibly extinct in the wild.
documentation.habitats: The taxon is an erect or ascending perennial herb found in several habitat types, such as montane wet, dry, and mesic forest; montane-subalpine mesic; and dry shrubland and grassland, including on barren lava.
documentation.threats: The major threats to this taxon include predation and habitat degradation by non-native animals, particularly feral pigs (Sus domesticus), goats (Capra hircus), cattle (Bos taurus), mouflon (Ovis orientalis), and deer (Axis axis), which degrade the habitat and harm the plants through predation, trampling, and rooting for food. Rats (Rattus rattus) pose a threat to the species through predation of the plant and its fruits; and introduced slugs and snails threaten the species by feeding on its leaves, stems, and seedlings. Alien plants also threaten the species by altering its habitat and competing with it for moisture, nutrients, light, and space.
documentation.measures: <span id="docs-internal-guid-08b3ff14-7fff-0257-e111-96a5cf1491a7">The taxon is on the U.S. Endangered Species List and the State of Hawaiʻi Endangered Species List. There are no known plants remaining in the wild but the species  is a survey target for the Hawaiʻi State Division of Forestry and Wildlife and the Hawai’i Plant Extinction Prevention Program.
documentation.rationale: Ranunculus hawaiensis is assessed as Critically Endangered - Possibly Extinct in the Wild. The taxon is endemic to the islands of Maui and Hawaiʻi and has not been observed in the wild since 2014. It has experienced severe and ongoing decline in habitat and numbers due to the impacts of invasive plants and animals. If it is still extant, the surviving population is estimated to be below 50 mature individuals. This qualifies the taxon to a ranking of Critically Endangered - Possibly Extinct in the Wild under criterion D.

documentation.range: This species is endemic to the Hawaiian Islands, found between 260 and 915 m elevation on the island of Kauaʻi (Wagner et al. 1999). It is Possibly Extinct in the Wild. The National Tropical Botanical Garden manages outplantings in the Lower Limahuli Preserve restoration site.
documentation.population: This taxon is Possibly Extinct in the Wild. It is known historically from scattered localities on Kaua'i (Lammers, 2005). The National Tropical Botanical Garden manages an outplanting site of approximately 100 individuals in the Lower Limahuli Preserve restoration site.
documentation.habitats: The taxon is a shrub found in Hawaiian mesic forest dominated by Metrosideros polymorpha. The two historic known localities where it formerly occurred are composed of scattered, relict native canopy and a predominately non-native understorey.
documentation.threats: The major threats to this taxon include direct competition by invasive non-native plant species, especially Melaleuca quinquenervia, Cyathea cooperi, Melinis minutiflora, Andropogon glomeratus, Lantana camara, and Clidemia hirta and predation by non-native animals, particularly feral ungulates (feral pigs, Sus domesticus; feral goats, Capra hircus and Mule Deer, Odocoileus hemionus; USFWS, 2008) that destroy the habitat and plants directly. Severe damage has been observed to stems, fruits and seeds from slugs and non-native rodents. Germplasm production is often interrupted due to the loss of native pollinators, both bird and insect. Seed dispersal cycles have also been greatly reduced due to the drastic decline of endemic avian fauna. In addition, the taxon is also threatened by diseases transmitted by leafhoppers and spider mites (USFWS 2008).
documentation.measures: The taxon is on the US Endangered Species List, and also on the State of Hawaiʻi Endangered Species List. Ex situ cultivation and seed storage is ongoing. The National Tropical Botanical Garden has and continues to undertake ex situ conservation work through the growing of plants in the Living Collections and Horticulture Nursery and outplanting in the Lower Limahuli Preserve fenced restoration site.
documentation.use_trade: There are no known uses for this species.
documentation.rationale: Delissea rhytidosperma is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in Wild) under criteria C and D. The taxon is endemic to the island of Kauaʻi. This taxon was last observed in Hanakapiai on 1/1/2002 (USFWS 2008).

documentation.range: When the species was first described in 1996, there were three known localities in the Soutpansberg region of the Limpopo province and the size of the wild population was estimated to number between 400 and 500 plants.  Plants were recorded from 800 to 1,000 m asl. By 2004 the monitored wild population had declined to 219 plants and today there are no confirmed specimens of this species remaining in the wild.
documentation.population: The population has declined from an estimated 400-500 plants when it was first described. None of the plants of this species that were counted in repeat helicopter surveys have survived. The species occurs in rugged mountainous terrain so it is possible that some specimens might remain.
documentation.habitats: Plants grow exposed on southeast-facing quartzite cliffs, in moist semi-deciduous mixed scrub. The rainfall is between 350 and 650 mm per annum. The vegetation type is mainly Mountain Bushveld.
documentation.threats: This species has effectively been extirpated in the wild due to over-collecting for ornamental purposes.
documentation.measures: This species is listed in Appendix I of the CITES Appendices. Plants used to occur in the Makuya Nature Reserve. Identification of suitable sites for the formal protection/restoration/recovery of this species is needed.
documentation.use_trade: This species is threatened due to over-collecting for ornamental purposes.
documentation.rationale: Encephalartos hirsutus is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) (CR(PEW)). The original population (at the time of description) was estimated at 400–500 plants. In 2004, only 219 plants were found in two localities as part of helicopter surveys, with most of the plants occurring in one site. S. Rogers (pers. comm.) from the Limpopo Provincial government reported in 2006 that ground rangers could not locate these plants and that they were assumed to have been removed. By 2020, none of the known specimens of E. hirsutus could be located. Parts of the original range comprise rugged mountainous terrain and it is possible that other specimens exist and there are ongoing surveys to locate and verify plants of this species.

documentation.range: Quercus albicaulis is native to China and is known to occur in only one location in Hainan province. The locality is now in the centre of the capital city of Sanya and is most likely destroyed.
documentation.population: Quercus albicaulis has only three recorded occurrences, all within one threat-based location in Hainan, China. Recent survey trips have been unsuccessful in locating the species and it is possible that the species no longer exists in the wild.
documentation.habitats: Quercus albicaulis occurs in mixed mesophytic forests in Hainan, China.
documentation.threats: The species is threatened by restricted distribution and habitat destruction. Quercus albicaulis occurs in natural forest areas in Hainan province which is threatened by habitat destruction. A 2015 study by Zhai et al. found that Hainan province has seen a loss in natural forest area and an increase in rubber plantation area from 1995 to 2005. The study noted that the trend occurred in protected areas as well. The loss of natural forest and increase in area for rubber plantations leads to habitat destruction and fragmentation for species that rely on natural forest habitat. The species could also be vulnerable to local fuel-wood collecting.
documentation.measures: The type locality for Quercus albicaulis in Sanya city needs to be visited to ascertain site status. If lost, an intensive field-survey of protected areas in the immediate vicinity of Sanya (by specialists for Quercus albicaulis) could reveal additional individuals of this rare species, and allow for urgently required ex situ propagation measures. Quercus albicaulis is not currently recorded in any ex situ collections (BGCI 2020). The species has been assessed as Critically Endangered in the Red List of China.
documentation.use_trade: There is little information on the use and trade of this species, but it could be vulnerable to local fuel-wood collecting.
documentation.rationale:
Quercus albicaulis is known to occur in only one threat-based location in county Ya Xian, Hainan, China. However, there have been no recent records and it is considered Possibly Extinct. The area in which the species occurs in Hainan has experienced a reduction in natural forest area which threatens the habitat of the species. Due to the limited extent of occurrence (EOO: 4 km2) and area of occupancy (AOO: 4 km2), the number of locations (1), and inferred threats to the species' habitat, it is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct).

Future research should focus on surveying the species to ensure that it has not gone extinct in the wild, enforcing protections to natural forest habitat, and increasing ex situ conservation of the species. The species is in need of additional information regarding its population, habitat quality, and ongoing threats, as well as future monitoring of the population.

documentation.range:
This species is endemic to Fiji where it is only present on the island of Taveneuni (Thompson and Braglia 2017). This small tree grows at high elevations exceeding 1,000 m asl.

Due to increasing scarcity of this species its area of occupancy is not anticipated to exceed 12 km2 when calculated with a 2 x 2 km grid and extent of occurrence is estimated to be 12 km2. The species is present in one location as all remaining individuals will be affected by equivalent threats.
documentation.population:
During three survey visits to Taveuni in 2016 and 2017 no wild Hibiscus storckii individuals were found. In 1997/8 a single plant was observed in Somosomo but this individual is assumed to have been destroyed due to the establishment of a dalo (Colocasia esculenta) garden; this plant has not been found again in all recent surveys. Further observations within Tavuki village from 2014 were not confirmed during the 2016/17 surveys. It is therefore concluded that the species is increasingly uncommon and considerably rare. In certain parts of the species range on Taveuni the species is considered extinct for example on Des Voeux Peak where it has not been sighted since a Category 5 storm in 2016 (Thompson and Braglia 2017). Due to this, the number of remaining individuals (if any remain) is anticipated to be well below 50.

Prior to the anticipated loss, the population was fragmented across mountain peaks exceeding an elevation of 700 m (Thompson and Braglia 2017).
documentation.habitats:
Hibiscus storkii is a small tree or shrub, between 2 and 4 m in height. It grows within upland rainforest and cloud forest of the Cakaudrove province, Fiji. Hence the species is tolerant of low light levels and high humidity. The species grows in association with Astronidium sp., Blechnum milnei, Cyathea alata, Cyathea medularis, Cyrtandra tempestii, Ficus vitiensis, Freycinetia sp., Macaranga seemannii, Medinilla waterhousei, Plerandra sp., Scaevola floribunda, Smilax vitiensis, Spiraeanthemum serratum and Weinmannia richii (Thompson and Braglia 2017). 

Within Fiji this habitat type is at risk from climate change, which is causing the area of remaining cloud forest to shrink.
documentation.threats: The occurrence of this species in an already restricted area makes it very susceptible to threats. The species is currently at risk from climate change which, could cause shrinkage of the already fragmented habitat. The planting of Miscanthus floridulus (Labill.) Warb. ex K.Schum. & Lauterb., a native reed, to control erosion on some peaks puts Hibiscus storckii at risk and may limit regeneration, due to the clumped stands which the introduced species produces. As the species is no longer present on Des Voeux Peak following Category 5 TC Winston in 2016, it also appears that the species is at risk from severe weather events (Thompson and Braglia 2017).
documentation.measures: Hibicus storckii is not present in ex situ collections (BGCI 2018). It is recommended that the species is bought into collections as a priority if re-discovered in the wild. The species should also be secured within in situ conservation sites and it should be ensured there is cultivation and propagation of the species from any collected individuals (Thompson and Braglia 2017).
documentation.use_trade: This species can be cultivated in home gardens in some parts of Fiji, Tonga and Samoa but this is not common. There is no further use of or trade in this species.
documentation.rationale: Hibiscus storckii is an exceedingly rare plant endemic to the island of Taveuni, Fiji. During field surveys in 2016/17, wild individuals of the species could not be found despite previous observations of the species from 1997/8 and 2014. It is anticipated that this species may be extinct in the wild. This plant has experienced pressure from climate change on its native cloud forest habitat and also from introduced species and severe weather events. Hibiscus storckii is predisposed to risk as its population was fragmented between mountain tops and it occurred within a very small geographic range which shrank due to habitat fragmentation and loss. The species is globally assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild). If individuals of this species are found it is essential that they are collected, protected and propagated.

documentation.range:
Two subspecies of White Rhino are currently recognized, the Northern (NWR) and the Southern (SWR), each having a strikingly discontinuous range in recent times. However there is fossil evidence the species used to have a continuous distribution and there is genetic evidence of probable post divergence secondary contact during the last interglacial (14,000 to 26,000 years ago) facilitated by savanna grassland expansion at that time (Moodley et al. 2018).

The Northern White Rhino (NWR) used to range over parts of northwestern Uganda, southern Chad, southwestern South Sudan, the eastern part of Central African Republic, and northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (Sydney 1965). The previous only confirmed subpopulation in Garamba National Park in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo is now considered probably extinct. Despite systematic ground surveys over probable range and additional foot patrols and aerial reconnaissance no live rhinos have been seen since 2006 and no fresh sign since 2007. There continue to be unconfirmed reports/rumours of rhino in southern Sudan but these have not been reliably confirmed and wildlife poaching in this area has reportedly increased and so it is unlikely any still survive. The last four potential breeding Northern White Rhino in captivity in Dvur Kralove Zoo in the Czech Republic were translocated to a private conservancy in Kenya in the hope this would stimulate their breeding but despite mating no offspring were produced before the two old males died, and it appears the females will not breed despite attempts at inter-crossing. These two non-breeding females form the only current confirmed living NWR but cannot be included in the Red List assessments as they have not bred since reintroduction back into the wild.

Note: At the request of certain members and countries, the IUCN SSC African Rhino Specialist Group (AfRSG) has a policy of not releasing detailed information (including maps) showing the whereabouts and names of all rhino subpopulations for security reasons. For this reason, only whole countries of occurrence are indicated on the range maps produced by the AfRSG.
documentation.population: In the only confirmed surviving wild subpopulation in Garamba National Park, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Northern White Rhino (Ceratotherium simum cottoni) numbers declined rapidly from 30 in April 2003 due to an upsurge in poaching, and surveys in 2006 confirmed the presence of only four rhinos (Emslie et al. 2006). Numbers are believed to have stood at around 2,360 in 1960 (Emslie and Brooks 1999). However, based largely on extensive and systematic foot surveys which failed to sight live rhino and find any signs (spoor and dung) this subpopulation is now considered probably extinct. Reports of a few possible Northern White Rhino surviving in a remote part of South Sudan have yet to be confirmed. The last four potential breeding Northern White Rhino in captivity were moved to a private conservancy in Kenya in the hope that a move to more wild conditions would stimulate them to breed. While the two females came into oestrus and mated no calves have been born and the two males have subsequently died. Assisted reproductive methods are being developed in the hope of being able to conserve some Northern White Rhino genes.
documentation.habitats: The subspecies was found in grassland in bushveld savanna habitats. It is a grazer.
documentation.threats:
Poaching and civil wars in both Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighbouring South Sudan had a devastating impact on Northern White Rhino. Whilst poaching pressure initially increased during civil unrest and war in the late 1990s, good reproduction enabled the population to remain relatively stable. However, since 2003, poaching escalated and the population declined rapidly with 11 carcasses found in a three-month period between March and May 2004. Confirmed numbers of Northern White Rhino fell from 30 individuals in April 2003 to just four in August 2005. No live rhino have been seen since 2006 or signs of live rhino (spoor or dung) reported since 2007 despite intensive systematic foot surveys. It is believed that the Northern White Rhino has probably gone extinct in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Rumours persist of possible survivors in war-torn South Sudan, but as yet there has been no conclusive evidence of this being the case. 

The survival of the subspecies is dependent on the development of assisted reproductive techniques; hence the current major threat to this taxon is if these techniques are unsuccessful.
documentation.measures: Any future conservation of adaptive Northern White Rhino (NWR) genes is dependent of successfully developing new assisted reproduction techniques. Researchers have collected oocytes from the two surviving NWR females and have sperm cells from five NWR that have all since died. The later could be used in IVF efforts. Advanced cellular techniques offer the potential to boost founder genetic diversity as there are stored cells and tissues from a greater number of NWR than for natural gametes. If Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) can be used to produce primordial germ cells, then there is a possibility to create oocytes and sperm from other dead NWR. If IVF can be successfully developed with embryos implanted in surrogate SWR mothers, then it should be possible to produce NWR calves. The latter when grown up could be used to create a self-sustaining population of rhinos. IVF inter-crossing could also be attempted. In time if such assisted reproductive methods can be successfully developed then once numbers have built up sufficiently some of these animals could eventually be reintroduced back into secure areas of former range or close to former range in East Africa. There can be no guarantee's such techniques will be successful but at this stage progress has been made in creating embryos in the lab.
documentation.use_trade: The subspecies was poached out in its last remaining confirmed wild population in Garamba National Park, the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
documentation.rationale:
The previous only confirmed wild subpopulation of the subspecies in the Garamba National Park and surrounding hunting areas in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo is now considered to have probably gone extinct. There have been no reported live sightings of any of the last four rhinos since 2006 or their signs since 2007 despite an intensive systematic ground search looking for rhinos and their signs in 2008. Additional aerial searches and field range patrols have also not found any remaining rhino although one carcass has been found. While there are reports of a small number possibly surviving in a remote area of South Sudan these have yet to be substantiated. The subspecies is therefore assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) pending further surveys for the species in South Sudan.

The only four potentially breeding rhino that were in Dvur Kralove Zoo in Czechia were moved to a private sanctuary in Kenya in the hope that the move to a more natural environment and natural diet and mixing with Southern White Rhino would encourage these animals to breed, but despite mating no offspring were produced before the two old males died, and it appears the females will not breed despite attempts at inter-crossing. These two non-breeding females form the only current confirmed living NWR but cannot be included in the Red List assessments as they haven't bred since reintroduction back into the wild. Any future conservation of adaptive Northern White Rhino (NWR) genes is dependent the success of current efforts to develop new assisted reproduction techniques (see Conservation Actions Information).
documentation.taxonomic_notes: While some researchers have proposed species status for both Northern (Ceratotherium simum cottoni) and Southern White Rhinoceros (hereafter White Rhino; Ceratotherium simum simum) (Groves et al. 2010), subspecies status was supported following comparison of whole mitochondrial genome sequences of  four Northern and three Southern White Rhino (Harley et al. 2016) and comparisons of nuclear and mitochondrial markers for a much larger sample size of extant and historical specimens dating back to the nineteenth century (Moodley et al. 2018).  Harley et al. (2016) estimated the time of divergence of NWR and SWR was in the range of 0.5 to 1 m years with the time of lineage splitting likely to be much more recent (possibly ~200,000 years). Eric Harley also found identical 10 base pair repeats, noting that as these tend to be unstable this is more in line with NWR being a subspecies rather than a separate species. He was critical of "species inflation" that can sometimes be derived using a phylogenetic approach to defining species (e.g. Mountain Zebra). A comparison of downloaded Mitochondrial DNA sequences from ten different humans revealed that modern humans differed from each other by a maximum of 0,7%. This level of difference was very similar to the 0.9% average difference he recorded between NWR and SWR and in line with treating NWR as a subspecies.  Moodley et al.'s (2018) analysis estimated time since divergence between the two WR lineages at approximately 0.97 m years with wide confidence levels of +/- 0.5m years. Both nuclear and mitochondrial markers structured the species into two distinct populations/clades (corresponding to NWR and SWR). However, Moodley et al. (2018)  also detected post divergence secondary contact between NWR and SWR and that this possibly occurred as recently as the last glacial maximum (14,000 to 26,000 years ago). Gene flow between the two populations will have been facilitated by grassland expansions at that time. In addition it might also prove desirable to try inter-crossing the subspecies as part of assisted reproductive efforts to recover and conserve some NWR genes. The IUCN SSC African Rhino Specialist Group continues to treat the two taxa as subspecies rather than separate species.

documentation.range: Endemic to the Hawaiian islands, between 1,010 and 1,525 m elevation on the islands of Molokai and Maui, but no wild plants are currently known from either island.
documentation.population: The taxon is extremely rare and possibly extinct.
documentation.habitats: The taxon is a scandent vine found in Hawaiian wet forest.
documentation.threats: The major threats to this taxon include direct competition by invasive non-native plant species, and predation and habitat degradation by non-native animals, particularly pigs, which degrade the habitat and harm the plants through predation, trampling, and rooting for food. Alien plants also threaten the species by altering its habitat and competing with it for moisture, nutrients, light, and space. Rats pose a threat to the species through predation of its plant parts and fruits; and introduced slugs and snails threaten the species by feeding on its leaves, stems, and seedlings. Fortini et al. (2013) characterized this taxon as extremely vulnerable to climate change (vulnerability index [0.62]).
documentation.measures: The taxon is on the U.S. Endangered Species List, and also on the State of Hawaiʻi Endangered Species List. This last known wild individual was recently observed to have died, but it is in cultivation and managed by the Hawaiʻi State Plant Extinction Prevention Program. Further research is needed on general ecology, life history, population size, distribution, trends and threats.
documentation.rationale: Phyllostegia mannii is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild). The taxon is endemic to the island of Maui and Molokai. It has experienced severe and ongoing decline in habitat and numbers due to the impacts of invasive plants and animals. The last remaining plant was recently reported to have died. This qualifies the taxon to a ranking of Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) under criterion B1ab(i,ii,iii,iv,v)+2ab(i,ii,iii,iv,v); D.

documentation.range: Magnolia wolfii is a species which is endemic to Colombia. The only population to have been reported was located in the town of Santa Rosa in the Risaralda department from the western slopes of the Central mountain range up to an altitude of approximately 1,800 m asl. There are only two hectares of remnant montane forest surrounded by coffee plantations where this species occurs.
documentation.population: The only population recorded for Magnolia wolfii consists of three mature individuals located in the town of Santa Rosa (Risaralda). The species is recorded only from the type locality in Risaralda. Based on a site visit carried out in August 2006 it appears that only three full grown trees and two saplings remain in a 2 ha remnant of forest surrounded by coffee plantations. Flowers and fruits are produced but no seedlings are recorded.
documentation.habitats: Magnolia wolfii is a canopy tree of sub-Andean humid cloud forests growing in fragments of primary and secondary forest located on steep slopes. It flowers and fruits in October. It is commonly known as 'hojarasco de Santa Roas' as its leaves are very thick and do not decompose very easily and therefore each adult plant is found surrounded by thick leaf litter.
documentation.threats: The original habitats of this region are in a constant state of deterioration principally due to the cultivation of coffee. The forests are severely fragmented and the patches very small and are surrounded by coffee plantations.
documentation.measures: It is possible that Magnolia wolfii occurs in the zone surrounding the Los Nevados National Park which neighbours the municipality of Santa Rosa de Cabal. Very little is known about this species and initially it was assumed that it was present in the Otun-Quimbaya Flora and Fauna Sanctuary but when this area was explored it could not be confirmed. It is suggested to evaluate the known remaining population to determine its conservation status and population structure and to offer some protection to this area as a reserve as an extension to the above mentioned reserves and develop protocols for the propagation of this species. M. wolfii is in ex situ collection in Colombia and the focus of research by Universidad Tecnológica de Pereira. This species is not known in cultivation. Its life history and reproductive capacity is being investigated with seed germination studied under natural and greenhouse conditions to facilitate future enhancement planting of seedlings in its natural habitat (Cicuzza, D. et al. 2007).
documentation.use_trade: There are no known uses or trade of Magnolia wolfii.
documentation.rationale: With only a single population of three mature trees and no regeneration observed in 2006, Magnolia wolfii is Critically Endangered due to habitat loss for coffee cultivation, occurring as an isolated forest fragment within extensive agriculture plantations. Its potential area of occupancy (AOO) and extent of occurrence (EOO) are both 0.2 km2, within a single location. It was classified as Critically Endangered in 1998. A survey is necessary to see if the three trees still exist, but it is likely that this species may now be extinct in the wild. More ex situ collections are required.

documentation.range: Gobiesox juniperoserrai is an endemic Nearctic freshwater species of Mexico, with a very restricted distribution, limited to the Pozas del Vado creek, Baja California Sur (Miller et al. 2005).
documentation.population: The only known specimens of Gobiesox juniperoserrai are the three type specimens collected at the time of discovery; the species is probably extinct (Ruiz-Campos et al. 2014).
documentation.habitats: The only stream where the species used to occur is seasonal, not permanent, usually 50 cm deep; the bottom is sand, gravel, rock, with vegetation dominated by Chara and Potamogeton (Miller et al. 2005).
documentation.threats: Gobiesox juniperoserrai is, or was, threatened by groundwater extraction (the stream where it used to dwell is spring-fed). Hence, the assessment by Jelks et al. (2008; Endangered) is sensible, and also coincides with the evaluation by Mexican environmental authorities (Diario Oficial de la Federación 2010). In addition, the locality faces invasion by the exotic fish Poecilia reticulata (Ruiz-Campos et al. 2014).
documentation.measures: No conservation actions for Gobiesox juniperoserrai exist, other than listing.
documentation.rationale: Gobiesox juniperoserrai is a microendemic desert species restricted to Pozas del Vado creek in Baja California Sur, Mexico. The species is severely threatened by over extraction of water resources and droughts caused by climate change. No specimens have been found since 1996, despite extensive search efforts from 2009 to 2014 (Ruiz-Campos et al. 2014). Considering its restricted range and continuing decline in the extent and quality of its habitat, the species is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct).

documentation.range: Stenogyne kanehoana was historically known from three populations, from 560 to 1,170 meters elevation, in the Wai'anae Mountains on O'ahu.
documentation.population: The taxon was known from three subpopulations on one island (O'ahu, Hawaiian Islands), but plants have since died, and no wild individuals have been recorded since 2013.
documentation.habitats: The taxon is a short-lived, perennial, scandent vine previously found in Hawaiian moist montane forests.
documentation.threats: The major threats to this taxon include direct competition by invasive non-native plant species, especially Clidemia hirta, Schinus terebinthifolia, and Psidium cattleianum, and predation by non-native animals, particularly rats, slugs, feral pigs, feral goats, and feral cattle. Ungulates also degrade habitat. In addition, the taxon is threatened by fire and an unidentified species of powdery mildew. It is also ranked as highly vulnerable to climate change (index 0.864 in Fortini et. al. 2013), due to loss of habitat.
documentation.measures: The taxon is on the US Endangered Species List, and also on the State of Hawai'i Endangered Species List. Ex situ cultivation is ongoing, and more reintroductions should be planned. More thorough surveys should be conducted at historical localities as well as new sites in similar and appropriate habitats to search for wild plants that may still exist.
documentation.use_trade: There are no known uses for this species.
documentation.rationale: Stenogyne kanehoana is assessed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild). The taxon is endemic to the island of O'ahu and has an extent of occurrence of zero km2 because there are no known wild plants in existence. This species has experienced severe and ongoing decline in habitat and numbers due to the impacts of invasive plants and animals. It was last observed in the wild in 2013, but is in ex situ cultivation and some individuals have been reintroduced. This qualifies the taxon to a ranking of Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) under criterion D.

supplementary_info.identification_information: Unmistakable bright yellow or orange frog with or without black spots or bands on dorsal surface. Difficult to distinguish from yellow forms of Atelopus varius.  Morphological differences between 5 ESU's  in the A. zeteki-varius clade are described in Zippel et al. 2006 and Richards & Knowles 2007.

documentation.range: This species is endemic to Panama, in the vicinity of the volcanic caldera of El Valle de Antón and Cerro Campana, between 335-1,315 m asl.
documentation.population: This species was once reasonably common at a number of localities, but it is now possibly extinct in the wild. The last wild individual was seen in 2009 (E. Griffith pers. comm. 2015). It disappeared from Cerro Campana and the central valley in El Valle de Antón likely due to over-collecting to supply the trade in live amphibians as pets. Remaining subpopulations have subsequently disappeared due to chytridiomycosis-related declines (McCaffery et al. 2015). Extensive ongoing monitoring at known sites by Project Atelopus have not found any surviving subpopulations, but further monitoring is needed (C. Richards-Zawaki and J. Voyles pers. comm. 2015). If a population still exists it is thought to have fewer than 50 mature individuals.
documentation.habitats:
It is a terrestrial species of tropical montane forest, with breeding and larval development taking place in forest streams. Males are known to perch on rocks and defend territories visually by by waving their arms in a semaphore behavior (Lindquist and Hetherington 1998). Egg strands 370 +/- 170 are laid in cool, flowing water and are attached to rocky substrates (Karraker et al. 2006). 

The species is aposematically colored and wild animals produce potent zetekitoxins that block sodium channels, but the toxicity is reduced or lost in captive conditions and may be derived from symbiotic microbial pathway linked to its diet (Daly et al. 1994, Yotsu-Yamashita et al. 2004).

Based on data from captive Atelopus populations, the generation length is estimated at 7 years (B. Gratwicke pers. comm. May 2018).
documentation.threats:
The major threat is chytridiomycosis, which has led to catastrophic population declines in this species (McCaffery et al. 2015) and many other wild populations of Atelopus (La Marca et al. 2005). In the wild, Bd-infected individuals were found basking in the sun, inducing a behavioral fever that may have helped them temporarily manage infections (Richards-Zawacki 2010). In the laboratory, disease is dependent on dose, environmental temperature, wetness and Bd strain but typically causes 100% mortality (Bustamante et al. 2010, Becker et al. 2012, Langhammer et al. 2013). In some experimental trials a few individuals were observed to clear infection. In one study, survivors were observed to share characteristic skin microbes compared to frogs that died (Becker et al. 2015). In a second study, when survivors were re-exposed to Bd they died, but preferentially expressed some immune-system linked genes that were not expressed in frogs that were naive (Ellison et al. 2014).

Deforestation of habitat for both agriculture and general infrastructure development, water pollution, and over collection for the pet trade are also threats to this species. It was once a popular pet and exhibit in hotels, and it is likely that the frogs were collected out from the Altos De Campana National Park, Panama long before chytridiomycosis arrived. Habitat quality is a major concern for this species due to rapid, ongoing residential development in the vicinity of El Valle de Anton. In 2003, a road from Sorá to El Valle was opened along the ridge of the Cordillera Central, resulting in heavy sedimentation of most streams on the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, which has negatively affected a significant portion of the habitat used by this species (R. Ibañez, in lit. to E. La Marca).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions In-Place
This species is protected in Panama by national legislation (as Atelopus varius zeteki) decree No. 23 of January 30, 1967, it was listed at CITES Appendix I in 1975, and Annex A in EU Wildlife Trade Regulations (2004) (CITES, 2013). In 2011, this species was identified as a very high priority species in Panama's amphibian conservation action plan (ANAM 2011). The only protected area within the former range of Panamanian golden frogs is Parque Nacional Altos de Campana, and it includes very little suitable habitat. In 2013 a stake-holder based workshop was held to develop a conservation action plan for the Golden Frogs of Panama (Atelopus zeteki and A. varius). The vision of the group  was "We are saving a national treasure, returning the Panamanian Golden Frog to nature" and conservation priorities are organized into working groups that include captive population management, disease management, habitat management, population viability analysis and communication and collaboration (Estrada et al. 2014).

A successful captive-breeding program in North America has been run by Project Golden Frog since 1999, and the Maryland Zoo in Baltimore is responsible for managing approximately 2,000 adult animals in 2 ESUs , including A. varius (Zippel et al. 2006, Poole 2006). These captive populations are formally managed by collection localities as Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) Species Survival Plans and pedigrees are closely tracked and managed to ensure retention of genetic diversity (Poole 2006, Estrada et al. 2014). A husbandry manual has been developed for this species (Poole 2006), that has been widely applied to the ex-situ conservation of other Atelopus species (Gratwicke et al. 2016). The species is displayed as a conservation flagship species in 50 zoos and aquariums in the US. In Panama, a small ex-situ population of this species is held at the El Valle Amphibian Conservation Center and the Panama Amphibian Rescue and Conservation Project in Panama (Estrada et al. 2014).

This species is an important national symbol in Panama. In 2010 a Panamanian law (Gazette No. 26592) designated August 14 National Golden Frog Day. The annual festival is anchored by a parade in the streets of El Valle De Anton every year that is organized by the Ministry of the Environment and the local community. Other events include family days, science talks, trail runs and museum days that attract thousands of participants each year (S. Ryan, Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute pers. comm.).

Conservation Needed
Continued loss of sites within the former range of this species means that options for reintroduction sites from captive populations are diminishing rapidly and protecting at least a few formerly occupied sites should be a priority if this species is to be reintroduced into the wild (Estrada et al. 2014).
documentation.use_trade: This species used to be sold in local markets as pets, and they were believed to be a symbol of luck. Figurines of this species can be bought in the El Valle market, and the animal has become a national emblem that can be found in many different settings.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) because of an observed drastic decline in population and extent of occurrence, due to chytridiomycosis combined with pressure from the pet trade, which is estimated to be more than 80% over the last 10 years. If a population remains in the wild it is thought to have fewer than 50 mature individuals.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Molecular data and morphological, ecological, and demographic analyses suggest that the Panamanian golden frogs and their kin (the Atelopus varius-zeteki clade) are comprised of five distinct forms (Zippel et al. 2006). Additional analyses identify phenotypic and genetic differentiation consistent with proposed Evolutionarily Significant Units (ESUs), and support the status of Atelopus varius and Atelopus zeteki as separate species (Richards and Knowles 2007). Atelopus zeteki distribution is limited to the vicinity of El Valle de Anton and Cerro Campana.

documentation.range: This species is found in xeric habitats of the Baja California Sur state in Mexico, particularly in the San Marcos and Del Carmen islands (Fryxell 1979). It occurs from sea level to 200 m asl.
documentation.population: There are two reported subpopulations of the species. The total number of individuals is unknown because the species has not been found in the last 10 years, neither in the original localities nor in potentially suitable habitat, even when field trips in different seasons have been carried out. It is, however, certainly less than 200 mature individuals.
documentation.habitats: The species is one of the most extreme xerophytes of the genus. It is a shrubby species that has evolved various xeromorphic adaptations, including a double palisade in the leaves (Fryxell 1979).
documentation.threats: The habitat of the species has deteriorated due to the introduction of goats and cats, as well as construction for touristic activities. The full extent of the consequences of these threats are unknown (A. Wegier pers. comm. 2017).
documentation.measures: It does not occur in any protected areas but efforts to eradicate goats from the areas in which it occurs have been taken. Ten germplasm accessions are stored in the USDA National Plant Germplasm System (Percy et al. 2014) but not in other genebanks (see e.g., Campbell et al. 2010).
documentation.use_trade: The species is not currently utilized. However, it is a tertiary wild relative of Cotton, Sea Island Cotton, Short-staple and Tree Cotton (USDA, ARS, GRIN 2017). It is a potential gene donor to these crops and has known potential to confer traits for pest resistance (USDA, ARS, GRIN 2017).
documentation.rationale: Gossypium armourinanum is assessed as Critically Endangered and may possibly be Extinct in the Wild because the species has not been found in the last 10 years, neither in the original localities nor in potentially suitable habitat, even when field trips in different seasons have been undertaken (A. Wegier pers. comm. 2017). If subpopulations still exist, the area of occupancy (AOO) is no more than 28 km2 and it is threatened by the introduction of goats that trample and degrade the habitat, as well as by construction for the tourism industry.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Gossypium armourianum Kearney is a tertiary wild relative of Cotton (G. hirsutum L.), Sea Island Cotton (G. barbadense L.), Short-staple Cotton (G. herbaceum L.) and Tree Cotton (G. arboretum L.) (USDA, ARS, GRIN 2017).

documentation.range:
Costus vinosus is known only from three locations in central Panama on the Caribbean side where there have been only 4 recorded collections.  The type was collected in 1973 along the Rio Guanche in Colon province at 50 metres but this area has experienced substantial habitat loss and several recent searches along the river have failed to find the plant still in existence there.  The last recorded collection there was in 1974. This assessor searched for C. vinosus in 2012, thoroughly checking small forest fragments remaining along the river, up river a distance of about five km and concluded that the species is no longer extant at this location.  Noted Marantaceae botanist Dr. Helen Kennedy told the assessor that her type specimen for Calathea gymnocarpa, which grows at the same low altitudes, has also disappeared from the Rio Guanche area due to conversion to pasture land.

The second location is a collection recorded in 1986 at 65 metres altitude along the "Rio Taindi (Taimdi on maps)" six km above the confluence with the Rio Mandinga. Based on the GPS coordinates given, this river is probably also known as Rio Cangandi on some maps. The determination was made by Greg de Nevers who was also the co-collector. Costus vinosus is a very distinctive species so this assessor has a high degree of confidence in the identification.

The third location is a collection recorded in 2004 at 250 metres altitude and a more inland location on the Santa Rita ridge of the Sierra Llorona.  This was collected and determined by Paul Maas who described the species in 1976.

With only two widely separated collection sites where the species is believed to exist, it is difficult to calculate an Extent of Occurrence (EOO) in square km.  A third point was set on the GeoCAT map to extend the area along the Rio Taindi where this species may still exist.  This resulted in an EOO calculation of 50 km2.  Based on the rarity of this species and the lack of other collection records, a two km wide square was used around these points to calculate the Area of Occupancy (AOO) of 12 km2.
documentation.population:
This species is believed to be gone from the area along the Rio Guanche where the type specimen was collected.  The last recorded collection was in 1974 and the area has since been deforested and converted to pasture land.  This assessor and others have searched for the species at Rio Guanche in the past several years without success. 

The Rio Taindi location collection was made in 1986 by Greg de Nevers and Heraclio Herrera.  Sr. Herrera was contacted by email and reported that he vaguely remembers the plant and it was not common in the Rio Taindi region.  He is the Director of Environment for the National Indigenous Peoples Coordinating Body of Panama, COONAPIP (Coordinadora Nacional De Los Pueblos Indígenas De Panama) and he knows the San Blas area well. He said he may have seen similar plants but could not say whether they were Costus vinosus.  He said, in his opinion, this species is gradually disappearing. 

The third collection at Santa Rita Ridge was made in 2004 by Dr. Paul Maas who first described the species in 1976 from the Rio Guanche population.  Dr. Maas has informed the assessor that he recalls observing only two to three plants in the Santa Rita subpopulation.

No other collection records have been found.  This is a very distinctive and noticeable species, and is likely to have been collected and recorded by botanists if it exists in any substantial populations.  Accordingly, this assessor is estimating the total population at less than 30 plants.

Costus vinosus is common in cultivation and used as an ornamental plant in gardens.  Based on experience in growing this species in cultivation, the assessor believes it would be particularly sensitive to habitat change. The species is known to be difficult to grow and bring to flower, very sensitive to cultural conditions and not prolific in flower and fruit. Since the last recorded collection was 10 years ago, and the collectors indicated there were few plants, it is possible that it is now extinct in the wild.
documentation.habitats: This species was described by Paul Maas as "Only known from the type locality in the province of Colon, Panama; in rocky vegetation in forest shade, near river; in same vegetation: Heliconia imbricata, Calathea silvicola, and Cyclanthus bipartitus; flowering in June; fruiting in August-September."
documentation.threats: The type locality is mostly converted to pasture land and only very small patches of secondary forest remain along the river at the lower altitudes where this species was found. The species is no longer thought to be in this area. The Santa Rita location has visible deforested areas surrounding it and is not in a protected area. There is a threat of further habitat destruction.  The third area (Rio Taindi) is the most remote and has the lowest threat.
documentation.measures: There is currently no active in situ conservation plans for this species, but it is common in cultivation is and held in the living collections of several botanical gardens. All these plants are believed to be clones from a single collection, and to be lacking genetic diversity.  There are no protected areas where this species is believed to be growing in the wild.  It is recommended that further field work be completed searching for this species in the two localities where it was last reported, and seeds collected for ex situ genome seed banks.  The species should then be reintroduced in a protected area in similar habitat and closely monitored.
documentation.use_trade: Costus vinosus is widely cultivated and used as an ornamental plant.  It is an especially attractive plant, prized by collectors.  The 1973 collection by Robert Dressler is known to have been cultivated at Lankester Gardens in Costa Rica.   An early accession record is at Marie Selby Botanical Gardens #1986-0224 indicates the plant received was from Dressler and was from Rio Guanche in Panama.  It is believed that further distribution to other botanical gardens and to the general public has resulted in its wide cultivation in the U. S. and no recent natural source for the cultivated plants has been found.
documentation.rationale: This species has only four recorded collections in 1973, 1974, 1986 and 2004 indicating it is rare in the wild. It has only been collected at three localities, one of which has been deforested and converted to pasture land with no plants still in existence there. At the other two localities, the collectors have informed this assessor that the species was not common and few plants were found.  The species is distinct enough from other Costus species that it would likely have more collections recorded by botanists if it existed in substantial subpopulations or other localities. The known localities are not in protected areas. The species is widely cultivated and well known to be difficult to grow and bring to flower indicating that it is sensitive to habitat change. Since the last collection record was ten years ago, it is possible that this species is extinct in the wild or very nearly so.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Costus vinosus was described by Paul Maas in 1976 from a single collection in 1973.  It is a very distinctive species with waxy leaves that have deep wine-red undersides and unique cup-shaped ligules making it very easy to recognize whether in flower or not.  There are no known taxonomic issues with this species.
